feedback: When several different sums all align with the same bar length, point out explicitly: different sums, same measure — that is what makes 5/6 flexible.

If a learner relabels a piece's denominator wrongly (e.g. calls a two-sixths piece '2/3'), rebuild that piece from sixth-sized units on the bar and recount: it is 2/6. A two-sixths piece does equal 1/3, but this task asks for same-denominator sums, so record every part in sixths.
If a learner can give only one break-up, prompt: 'Find a genuinely different way, then another' until two or more distinct valid sums appear.
Optional live interaction, where available: let cuts on the bar auto-write the matching sum and refuse any attempt to relabel a piece's denominator, so the reverse add-across cannot be recorded.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction is not one fixed break-up: any grouping of its unit parts that uses the same denominator and the same total count measures the same quantity. Addition joins those parts and subtraction separates them, while the unit stays fixed.
learnerActions: Start with a bar whose total length represents 5/6 of a whole, marked off into five equal sixths (each one-sixth of the whole) against a fixed ruler so its length cannot change.
Group the sixths one way (e.g. 1 and 4) and write the matching sum of sixths underneath: 5/6 = 1/6 + 4/6.
Regroup the SAME bar differently (2 and 3; then 1, 1 and 3) and write each new sum: 2/6 + 3/6, 1/6 + 1/6 + 3/6.
Line up all the sums you have written against the single unchanged bar and say aloud: 'all of these are 5/6'.
Repeat the whole process with a fresh fraction you have not seen (e.g. 7/8) to produce at least two distinct decompositions.
activities.title: Slice one bar many ways

feedback: If a learner writes 2 1/8 as 2/8 + 1/8, show each whole bar as 8/8 on the model and recount: two wholes are 16/8, so 16/8 + 1/8 = 17/8.
If the '2' is ignored, ask first 'How many eighths are in one whole? in two wholes?' before writing the conversion.
Reinforce by reversing it: start from 17/8 and build back the two whole eighths-bars plus one eighth.
activities.intendedInsight: A mixed number's whole part and fraction part are the same kind of unit part; the wholes can be recounted as eighths so the whole quantity is a single count of like parts (17/8).
learnerActions: Lay out 2 1/8 as two whole bars, each cut into eight eighths, plus one extra eighth.
Count the eighths in each whole bar (8/8 and 8/8), then join the extra eighth.
Write the quantity as a single count of eighths: 8/8 + 8/8 + 1/8 = 17/8, confirming the 2 wholes contribute 16/8, not 2/8.
State in words why the whole and the fraction are one quantity: 2 1/8 is seventeen eighths altogether.
activities.title: Mixed number as one count of like parts

feedback: For a learner who accepts 2/3+3/3: compute 2/3+3/3 (= 5/3, more than a whole) and compare to 5/6 — it is clearly not equal, and the pieces are not sixths.
Correct answer reference: 5/6 = any two distinct sums of sixths totalling 5/6 (e.g. 1/6+4/6 and 2/6+3/6); 2 1/8 = 8/8+8/8+1/8 = 17/8; the denominator stays fixed throughout.
Recognising a correct option is a check on reasoning; it does not by itself show the learner can build one, so always pair it with the learner producing their own second decomposition.
activities.intendedInsight: A valid same-denominator decomposition must keep the denominator fixed AND have parts that actually total the original fraction; the reverse add-across (2/3+3/3 because 2+3=5 and 3+3=6) produces parts that do not sum to 5/6.
learnerActions: Given several candidate sums for 5/6, decide which equal 5/6 and which do not — e.g. 1/6+4/6, 2/6+3/6, and the trap 2/3+3/3.
For each candidate, add the parts and compare the total to 5/6 to justify the decision, not just guess.
Explain why 2/3 + 3/3 fails: adding them gives 5/3 (more than a whole), not 5/6, and the parts are not measured in sixths.
Fill in a second valid decomposition of a given fraction, and match each mixed number to its improper form (e.g. 2 1/8 ↔ 17/8).
activities.title: Check and sort candidate decompositions

feedback: If a learner changes the denominator during subtraction, re-anchor on the unit: both numbers are sixths, so the answer is counted in sixths.
Ask the learner to verify by re-joining the result to the amount removed and checking they return to 5/6.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtraction separates like unit parts just as addition joins them; the denominator names the unit and stays fixed, so only the count of parts changes.
learnerActions: Show 5/6 − 2/6 on a bar or number line by separating two sixths from five sixths and reading the remaining three sixths.
Say in words what subtraction did: it separated two of the same unit parts, leaving 3/6; the denominator (sixths) did not change.
Connect it to joining: 3/6 + 2/6 rebuilds the original 5/6, so joining and separating are opposite moves on the same unit parts.
activities.title: Explain, don't just compute, subtraction as separating
